        The New York Giants are locking up one of their key figures on defense. On Tuesday, the team reached an agreement with cornerback Greg Newsome II on a three-year, $46 million extension, according to ESPN. The deal includes $32 million guaranteed. Newsome was playing on a one-year deal he inked with the franchise back in March, worth $8 million, so this uptick to an average annual value of $15.3 million is quite the raise for the 26-year-old. It's also a solid bargain for the Giants, as that AAV is outside the top-20 highest-paid corners in the NFL currently. Over this extension, Newsome is just under Lions corner D.J. Reed ($16 million in AAV) and just above Titans corner Cordale Flott ($15 million in AAV). In six games played this season for the Giants, Newsome has allowed 53.6% of his targets against to be completed, according to TruMedia. He's also surrendering just a 57.7 passer rating against, which is on pace to be a career high. For reference, his previous career low was a 73.2 passer rating, which he notched in 2023 and 2025 as a member of the Cleveland Browns. 
Nessome hasn't allowed a single touchdown so far this season and just two completions of 20-plus yards. He also has one interception. The Northwestern product initially entered the NFL in 2021 as a first-round draft choice (No. 26 overall) of the Browns. He spent the first four and a half years with Cleveland before being traded to the Jacksonville Jaguars in early October of last season. Newsome struggled in the Jags secondary, allowing five passing touchdowns over his 12 games played for the franchise. 
He's enjoyed a night-and-day difference in production with the Giants thus far, so it makes sense the two sides were eager to extend this one-year pact beyond 2026.

title: Barca's UCL dreams run through Lamine Yamal and Raphinha, and Aston Villa got a front row seat - CBS Sports
description: Lamine Yamal and Raphinha scored in a straightforward 3-0 win over Aston Villa, their third victory in four Champ
body:
Lamine Yamal and Raphinha scored in a straightforward 3-0 win over Aston Villa, their third victory in four Champions League games so far this season
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 3, 2026
                            
                    at
    6:28 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        There are normal ways to build up to a marquee UEFA Champions League match and there's Aston Villa, for whom the top searches under Google's news tab were all about being taken seriously. This was hardly an exercise in projecting confidence ahead of a trip to Barcelona; the club picked a fight with a broadcaster instead because, for some reason, they deemed he had the power "to stop our ascension in English and European football." Villa's year-over-year improvements are hard to deny, to the point that being somewhat competitive at the Camp Nou on Tuesday was not out of the question and they managed that much. There was just one problem, though.Punching above your weight is easier said than done against this version of Barcelona.Villa were no slouch but over the course of a 3-0 win on Matchday 4 of the Champions League, Barcelona were simply in cruise control. It is not that Villa did not pose a challenge – they sparked at times in the first half, Johan Manzambi responsible for the visitors' best chance of the game around the half-hour mark. There was simply nothing they could do at the Camp Nou, their ascension irrelevant even if it is true, because Barcelona are as close to the summit as it gets.Barcelona barely put a foot wrong as they strung together a trademark performance, well-positioned to do the easy things when the time called for them. That was true as soon as the seventh minute when Joao Gomes, under very little pressure, played a perfect pass to Lamine Yamal with plenty of space in front of him. Even as a couple of Villa defenders tried to close the space near goal, Yamal found his crevice and finished the chance off. It was perhaps the easiest way for him to score his 14th Champions League goal, surpassing Kylian Mbappe as the teenager with the most goals in the competition.
The hosts overwhelmed Villa's defense with ease, Yamal's goal merely the first sign of trouble for the visitors. Raphinha bagged a 12-minute brace in the second half, the entire collection of goals a remarkable example of defensive errors. There's a comedy to the Brazil international's first goal, something casual about his strike despite three Villa defenders in his vicinity, watching the ball as it flew into the back of the net. On his second, Joao Cancelo was essentially given permission to dance around Villa's defense to find a Raphinha that was virtually unmarked and converted again from close range.
The mistakes from Villa were glaring, almost obfuscating Barcelona's performance entirely. It was not simply a walk in the park, though – Hansi Flick's side got to roll out Plan A and showcase its strengths fully, the lopsided result reflecting the more subtle elements of their dominance. They were able to possess exactly as they wanted to, taking 16 shots and generating 1.99 expected goals along the way. Their attacking might is hardly a surprise now that Raphinha is several years into a career revitalization steered by Flick and now that Yamal is already well known as the sport's next great talent.What was more impressive was their ability to completely shut Villa out, especially so considering the circumstances. The game state was not exactly a deterrent to Unai Emery's side – 10 days earlier, they let Manchester City have the ball and took their chances despite posting 0.61 expected goals and notched a 2-1 win in the process. Their total was a little better on Tuesday at Barcelona, generating 0.72 expected goals from nine shots, and this time they had the benefit of playing against an understaffed defense. A series of injuries have plagued Barcelona's back line in recent weeks, stripping a defense of the early season stability that had become a new trademark despite sticking true to the high line.
Villa, though, were unable to make much of a dent. Nicolas Jackson, who had eight goals in 12 games across all competitions before the trip to Barcelona, took just one shot on Tuesday. Any semblance of attacking threat never came through. Rodri was not exactly some great denier, either – the captain of Spain's World Cup-winning team only played the first 45 minutes, earning the right to exit the game early after another job well done. Barcelona ensured Villa were dull over the course of 90 minutes; the defensive mistakes from the visitors were the end product rather than the cause of the hosts' success.On a day where Villa's ascension was cast aside, Barcelona's rise was hard to miss. The gap they are trying to make up is smaller and easier to envision but it does not mean that Flick's side does not carry a certain amount of baggage on each and every Champions League night. They are 11 years removed from the last time they won Europe's top title, a lengthy stretch for one of the game's most celebrated teams. Self-imposed financial hardship has hindered their progress but since Flick took the job two years ago, they have inched closer and closer to the winner's medals they have been eager to collect.Beating Paris Saint-Germain, the undeniable favorites after back-to-back titles, to the podium is another question entirely, especially after a 4-2 loss in the French capital on Matchday 3. Flick, though, insisted that day was merely a step on the journey, an experience to learn from as they attempt to ascend up Europe's ranks themselves. Champions often make their case on difficult days and should Barcelona make a deep run, they will likely have the chance to do just that down the stretch. The road to the Champions League title, though, usually includes some impressively unfussy days and on Tuesday, Flick's side collected one.

title: Why Bears' Caleb Williams gave up his fight against the NFL over his unapproved cleats - CBS Sports
description: For the first time this season, Caleb Williams actually followed the NFL's uniform policy
body:
For the first time this season, Caleb Williams actually followed the NFL's uniform policy
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 3, 2026
                            
                    at
    4:02 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        After taking on the NFL over the past two weeks and getting hit with more than $35,000 in fines, Caleb Williams has finally given up the fight over his cleats. During Chicago's 34-17 win over the Seahawks on Monday, Williams covered up the logo on his Caddix cleats for the first time this season. Following the game, the Bears quarterback said he gave in because he didn't want it to be a distraction anymore. "Just to calm things down," Williams said after the game. "It was a big week and not here to create any B.S. towards the team. I want to keep that to a minimum from my side. Obviously I get a lot of media and so just trying to minimize that as much as possible."All eyes were on Williams going into Monday's game because he was heading into uncharted territory. Under NFL rules, there are only three companies that currently have a partnership with the NFL — Nike, Adidas and Under Armour — and the logos from those three companies are the only ones that are allowed to be on the field during a game. 
Players are allowed to wear a pair of cleats from a different company, but if they go that route, they have to cover up the logo. Williams has been wearing his Caddix cleats all season and the NFL finally hit him with a $11,941 fine in Week 6. In Week 7, not only did Williams wear the cleats again, but once again, he knowingly violated NFL protocols by not covering up the logo. The league responded by hitting him with a $23,882 fine. After being fined $35,823 over two weeks, Williams still wasn't ready to back down. In the lead-up to Monday's game against the Seahawks, he actually told ESPN that he would not be covering the logo on his cleats. The problem with that plan is that the NFL is actually allowed to keep a player from participating in a game if the player keeps violating the league's uniform policy, so there was a chance that Williams wouldn't be allowed to play if he didn't cover up his cleats for Monday's game. Williams clearly got the message, because when he came out for warmups, the Caddix logo was covered up. 
Bears coach Ben Johnson was asked about the cleat controversy over the weekend and he seemed pretty confident that his star QB was going to make the right decision. "He's all about the team and I know he's not going to hurt the team," Johnson said last Saturday.Williams wears the Caddix cleats because he thinks they're safer than other brands. 
"As we've known for the past couple of years now, I'm huge into my body, I'm huge into trying to stay on the field, I'm huge into trying to be healthy," Williams said last week. "It's a rough game and things like that. The cleats, they've been great, they've been super comfy and they've worked. They are a science type of cleat."The Caddix cleats, which are known for their patented "SmartStuds" technology, are now worn by dozens of NFL players. Joe Flacco was the first NFL player to wear them back in 2024, and he liked them so much that he's now an investor in the company. He actually offered to pay any fines that Williams might incur for getting them. Caddix also offered to pay the QB's fines, according to ESPN, so there's a good chance that the Bears QB won't end up losing out any money despite getting fined more than $35,000.

        The Buffalo Bills have released veteran safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson, the team announced on Tuesday. This split comes in the wake of Gardner-Johnson coming back from the one-game suspension that he served in Week 8 due to a spitting incident that occurred in Week 6 against the Las Vegas Raiders. Gardner-Johnson, who signed a one-year deal worth $6 million with Buffalo back in March, was spotted by NFL on CBS cameras spitting in the direction of Raiders tight end Brock Bowers and center Tyler Linderbaum. That led to him being flagged for unsportsmanlike conduct and being ejected from the game.That also led to the NFL handing down a one-game suspension on the 28-year-old, which he served during last Sunday's win over Baltimore following Buffalo's Week 7 bye.
While this incident probably didn't help his case to remain on the team, ESPN reports that this release had more to do with his inconsistent play in the secondary. Specifically, the report noted that the organization felt like there were too many "what the hell is he doing" plays. Through six games played this season, Gardner-Johnson has allowed a 64.7% completion rate and an 83.5 passer rating against. Last week, Damar Hamlin started in place of Gardner-Johnson, and he should be looked at as the favorite to take over that spot going forward. In the win over Baltimore, Hamlin totaled five tackles and a pass defended. 
The Florida product entered the NFL as a fourth-round draft choice of the New Orleans Saints back in 2019. He spent his first three seasons of his career with the franchise before being traded to the Philadelphia Eagles in the summer of 2022. Gardner-Johnson has since bounced around the league, making stops with the Lions, Texans, Ravens, and Bears before arriving in Buffalo this offseason.

        If this feels like vindication for Manchester United, it shouldn't. The sort of unforgettable European night you could have been forgiven for thinking might be a long time in coming for this listing club, certainly. A fresh start to a season that seemed on the brink, perhaps. And yet everything else does not go out of the window just because this team made Old Trafford roar again in a thrilling comeback to beat Roma 3-2.A modicum of the commitment, energy and application they showed in the second half and United would never have been in the hole they found themselves in in the first. It turned out that when United do not just throw in the towel on the concession of a goal, there's still a decent football team lurking in there. More significantly than that, there are players who are still committed to the cause and perhaps to the manager. It surprised many that Michael Carrick got the backing of those above him after the defeat to Bournemouth nine days ago. This was as clear an indication as any that his players share his commitment to the cause, the belief he articulated on Monday.Carrick might, however, ask where exactly this had been on the many occasions adversity came United's way in the last month. Why has everyone not been playing with the ferocity that Matheus Cunha used to carry this team back from the brink? The Brazilian was so exceptional you could forgive the overexuberance of a late red card. It was the same quality that saw him force the penalty through which the petulant Bruno Fernandes halved the deficit. The equalizer was afforded to Cunha when Leonardo Balerdi cleared fresh air. The winner only required a helping hand from Shea Lacey, Cunha taking the ball to a narrow angle and rocketing in a goal that seemed unimaginable when the hosts were being booed to the dressing room at the interval.Old Trafford had been electrified. It hadn't taken much, that penalty where Fernandes was lucky to get a second chance after a questionable encroachment call. When Bryan Mbeumo clipped both posts, it sounded like the wobbly roof might come off. All it had taken was a few minutes of intensity and a browbeaten crowd roared again. Hope can now spring at a ground that really wants to believe that Carrick can get this right.
And yet whether he can will remain in doubt when so many of his players can fail to execute a game plan for so long, as they did in defeat at Como last month. That much was apparent for Roma's first goal. It was evidently part of Carrick's tactical plan to get Diogo Dalot high up the field early in the move to apply pressure to the right wing back. Risky, given the threat Matias Soule posed at the other end, but a perfectly valid approach. What would be required is some willingness on the part of others to plug gaps if Roma turned the ball over at the right moment.Make no mistake, Dalot, stood with gray shirts between him and the ball, was not really making himself available for the pass. When Roma turned the ball over, however, the left back did blitz it back into position. There was just no way for him to get back in time. For Fernandes, perhaps there were gaps he could plug. Kobbie Mainoo too could have got in position. Instead, the right half of the penalty area was wide open for Soule to collect a pass from Rodrigo Mora and drive past Senne Lammens.This is the sort of goal that, once you have conceded once, you ought never to again. Strictly speaking, United didn't; it is just that the penalty they conceded five minutes later again came because no one was filling the space vacated by Dalot. This time Soule tried to turn provider before getting the ball back off a lackadaisical Harry Maguire clearance. His shot deflected off Ayden Heaven's arm, Donyell Malen doubling the lead from the penalty spot.
The 28 minutes that followed were perhaps even more troubling. The legends of this football club are forged in fighting spirit on European nights, and yet defeat seemed to be accepted. United did not manage to take a shot in the penalty area in the first half. Amad Diallo seemed to be the only man who could get the ball into those dangerous areas. Meanwhile Fernandes carped at Carlos Baleba over a pass he didn't like. Baleba gave it back too. United looked to be on the brink.It speaks favorably of Carrick that he turned it around not through any obvious tactical adjustments but through getting his side to move the ball with a little more intensity. They delivered it, and at the club that Sir Alex Ferguson built, there will always be a belief that a manager can come back from the brink to reach footballing immortality.And yet the common thread of recent weeks is not that United can be as good as they were in the second half but that they can consistently plumb the depths they hit in the first. It only takes Morgan Rogers running in a straight line, Nico Paz finding space or Leny Yoro slipping to begin a chain reaction of mental anguish. On the evidence of tonight, those momentary crises were never intractable. Doesn't that make it all the more infuriating that United players were the first to call it quits?

        Another Champions League matchday is partially in the books. There are some teams that are already halfway through the league phase, which will last until January. It's important to remember that only the top eight teams will qualify directly for the knockout rounds, while those finishing between ninth and 24th place will have to compete in a two-legged playoff in February to secure their place in the next stage. Let's now take a look at some of the big European teams and see how much they should be worried ahead of the remaining four league phase games. AS Roma The Giallorossi lost again in the final minutes of a Champions League match. Gian Piero Gasperini's side repeated the same mistakes they made last month at the Stadio Olimpico against Real Madrid, when they conceded three goals late in the second half after being up 3-1. Something similar happened against Manchester United at Old Trafford, as AS Roma lost 3-2 after scoring the first two goals of the game. Next up is a trip to PSG at the Parc des Princes, and it's difficult to imagine them bringing any points back to Rome. With four points collected after four games, they should start to worry a bit now. Panic level: 7/10 😤Atletico MadridThey are in a better spot than AS Roma. Diego Simeone's side have been quite disappointing so far, losing to Liverpool away and to Bayern Munich at home, though they did beat Manchester United in Madrid earlier. Clearly, they had a very challenging first half of the league phase, but they now have a much more doable path: Viking, PSV and Bodo/Glimt, before facing Fenerbahce in their last away game of the league phase. They should aim to finish in the top 16 at the very least.Panic level: 6/10 🤕InterAfter defeats against Real Madrid and Club Brugge in the opening two games of the league phase, the Nerazzurri won two in a row against Shakhtar and, most notably, 3-0 away at Feyenoord. That win came a few days after Inter lost the Derby della Madonnina 3-1 to AC Milan, a defeat that raised many doubts about Cristian Chivu's management following some disappointing performances early in the season. However, the win against Feyenoord put things in a much better place for Inter, who will now host Stuttgart at San Siro before facing Borussia Dortmund away, Liverpool in Milan and Slavia Prague in the final match of the league phase.Panic level: 5/10 🤩Man UnitedOn the other hand, things finally look a bit better for Manchester United after beating AS Roma at Old Trafford. However, the big question now is: has Michael Carrick left it too late? Things will be clearer in the coming days, especially ahead of the November international break. The Red Devils have some challenging matches left in the league phase, with visits to Sporting CP and Villarreal plus home games against RB Leipzig and, most notably, Bayern Munich. It's certainly not over for them yet, but at least they can now look ahead with a little more optimism.
Panic level: 6/10 😡

body:
Joe Fagnano will make his first NFL start Thursday against the Jaguars, with Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley likely headed to injured reserve
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 3, 2026
                            
                    at
    4:29 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Baltimore Ravens will start undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano when they host the Jacksonville Jaguars in the Week 9 opener on Thursday night, coach Jesse Minter announced. Fagnano's ascension to QB1 comes in the aftermath of injuries taking a massive toll on the Ravens depth chart, with Lamar Jackson suffering a right thumb injury that required surgery, along with top backup Tyler Huntley dealing with a turf toe injury. "We'll be starting Joe at quarterback this week on Thursday," Minter said. "An opportunity we're fired up about. Excited to play in front of our fans Thursday night against a really good team." Fagnano was the emergency third quarterback when the Ravens kicked off their Week 8 matchup against the Buffalo Bills and found themselves needing to turn to him rather quickly. On the first snap of the day for the Baltimore offense, Jackson injured his right thumb on a follow-through, colliding with Buffalo pass rusher Greg Rousseau. That knocked him out of the game and thrust Huntley into action. However, he was unable to stay on the field long after suffering the toe injury. Minter noted that Jackson and Huntley are likely heading to injured reserve before Thursday's game, so this start against Jacksonville could be the first of many for Fagnano. Kicker Tyler Loop is also set to land on I.R. 
Coming in under duress last week, Fagnano completed 10-of-21 for 91 yards and an interception, while also losing a fumble. The 25-year-old rookie with Baltimore in the spring after going undrafted in the 2026 NFL Draft out of UConn. Over the course of the summer, he beat out fellow undrafted rookie Diego Pavia to make the opening 53-man roster. "Going all the way back, it's a guy that took advantage of opportunities," Minter said of Fagnano. "When we talked in training camp about, really [to] all 90 players that you have at that time, having a chance and you can play your way onto the team, I really thought he did that. "He didn't get a ton of reps in OTAs due to our numbers at quarterback, especially days when we had all of those guys there. Truthfully, when we had an injury at the position, you know, 10 days before our first preseason game, he started to get more reps. Then, we all obviously saw how he played in the game."
In the preseason, he completed 56-of-75 (74.7%) for 509 yards passing, three passing touchdowns, and one interception. Fagnano comments on ankle injury While Fagnano may be getting the nod, he may not be 100% healthy. During the loss to Buffalo, the UConn product appeared to injure his ankle, but was able to stay in the game. At practice on Tuesday, Fagnano was spotted wearing a rather large brace on that right ankle. 
"Good," Fagnano said when asked how his ankle is after practice. "Every game you got bumps and bruises. Just football. Physical game we play. Feels good, though."

The 43-year old Drinkwitz is 52-31 (29-26) overall at Missouri and 35-12 over the past four seasons. After the Texas game, Missouri plays at No. 2 Georgia before hosting No. 8 Kentucky and closing the regular season against Oklahoma.
Drinkwitz's name has come up in connection with other openings over the years as he's built Missouri into a steady SEC outfit. However, his extension last November, which came amid a coaching vacancy at Penn State, raised his average annual salary past $10.7 million. Drinkwitz is the 11th-highest paid coach in college football, according to the USA Today coaches salary databse. That means the list of programs which could realistically boost his pay is short.

title: MLB proposes delaying salary cap in new negotiations as Dec. 1 CBA expiration inches nearer - CBS Sports
description: In the league's new proposal, the salary cap would not be instituted until the 2028 season to give teams time to
body:
In the league's new proposal, the salary cap would not be instituted until the 2028 season to give teams time to prepare
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 3, 2026
                            
                    at
    3:59 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Major League Baseball has proposed delaying the implementation of a salary cap/floor system until 2028 as part of its latest collective bargaining agreement proposal, the league announced Tuesday. MLB says the delay is intended to provide a "smoother transition" to a salary cap/floor system and give teams more time to prepare and get their payrolls in order."We recognize that clubs will need a full offseason to prepare to operate within the cap and floor system. Therefore, with this offseason already underway, we proposed today to begin the cap and floor system in 2028," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "This proposal would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system without delaying key player benefits, including earlier free agency, a $1 million minimum salary, a 30% increase to the pre-arbitration bonus pool, and transactional reform that will reduce roster churn."The league also newly proposed a $180.2 million salary floor and a $258.2 million salary cap. Those numbers are up from $171.2 million and $245.3 million, respectively, in the league's previous proposal in June. The $1 million minimum salary would only apply to players with at least two years of service time. The minimum salary would be $900,000 for all other players.Four teams currently have more than $258.2 million on the books for 2027 (including arbitration projections) and 20 teams have less than $180.2 million on the books, according to FanGraphs' calculations. The current competitive balance tax and revenue sharing system would remain in place in 2027 before the transition to a salary cap/floor system in 2028.
The collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and the owners are expected to lock out the players at that time. The previous lockout ended on March 10, then there was a three-week spring training leading up to Opening Day. If there is a similarly lengthy lockout, it would be impossible for clubs to become salary cap-compliant in such a short period of time.The MLB Players Association has repeatedly insisted it will not accept a salary cap/floor system, and has instead proposed a revised revenue sharing system that would funnel more money from big-market teams to small-market teams. In a statement following the league's proposal on Tuesday, the MLBPA accused owners of continuing to "propose blowing up the current system and replacing it with one designed to line their pockets and increase their franchise values." The union also said that even with a delayed implementation, the league's proposal of a salary cap maintains the same "negative impacts," including a "massive reduction in player compensation" and the "elimination of fundamental player rights, including guaranteed contracts."
MLB says its push for a salary cap/floor system is intended to improve competitive balance. The small-market Milwaukee Brewers defeated the small-market Tampa Bay Rays in the World Series last week and swept big-market teams (Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Yankees) en route to the Fall Classic.

body:
The selection committee gave the SEC plenty of love with its new metric, leaving Notre Dame with no room for error and two-loss Alabama sitting way too high
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 3, 2026

    8:19 pm ET

            6 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Welcome to the first of five weeks of College Football Playoff frustration. The selection committee released its first Top 25 of the season Tuesday, and with five more to go until Selection Sunday, there's plenty to digest.Those who forget the past are doomed to repeat it, so a quick lesson before we overreact to the first rankings of the 2026 season. Last season taught us a clear lesson: never take a team's ranking at face value until Selection Sunday.It's easy to forget the magic trick the CFP pulled last fall, when they proved head-to-head results matter only when convenient. For five weeks, Miami trailed Notre Dame in the CFP's Top 25, even though the Hurricanes owned a head-to-head win in Week 1. On Selection Sunday, the CFP committee finally flipped the two, and Miami earned the final at-large spot in the playoff, jumping two spots despite not playing in the ACC Championship Game.Why? The committee's feelings — fueled by internal debate — were supported by their myriad metrics. Those metrics, by the way, are not available for public consumption.
On Tuesday night, we discovered a new metric that will fuel disruption: the strength-of-conference rating. Will that stick? History says no, because the committee changes its mind week to week. So, buckle up. If you're upset your favorite team is ranked lower than it deserves, or if you're frustrated that a rival is slotted higher than it deserves, don't fret. Both can change at any time, based on one of many lines of logic supported by endless proprietary data the CFP sees, but you don't.Feel hopeless? Don't! Embrace debate! The warning signs have been visible for years.
"Obviously, college football has the most passionate fan bases across the country," CFP selection chairman Hunter Yurachek explained mere moments after the CFP pushed Miami ahead of Notre Dame last December. "Everyone can spin the metrics in favor of the team or teams that they support. So you're always going to have controversy. "Here's what we didn't like about the first iteration of the CFP's Top 25 released Tuesday night, before an impactful Week 10 slate of games:For better or worse, the SEC's lobbying workedThe SEC lobbied hard over the last two years to introduce new metrics for the committee to use. Well, it worked. The strength-of-conference metric has apparently been the buoy that lifted the conference to heights no other power conference has been afforded. 
All six two-loss SEC teams are ranked higher than they are in both the AP and coaches polls this week. Two two-loss teams (No. 5 Alabama and No. 7 Texas) rank higher than undefeated UCLA at No. 8.Heck, the SEC has the highest-ranked two- and three-loss teams with Alabama and No. 21 South Carolina. If a 24-team playoff were played tonight, nine of 16 teams (!) from the SEC would be in the field.The issue here is the CFP said this new data point would be an enhancement, not necessarily a new metric, but it played out Tuesday as the biggest differentiator between the SEC teams and everyone else. The declaration when it was introduced months ago and the rankings released Tuesday do not match.
If this strength-of-conference metric continues to carry weight, expect some peeved-off fans in the other conferences at the end of the season.The committee continues to slight Notre DameIf it wasn't clear already, the Fighting Irish can't afford a loss this week against No. 1 Miami. Notre Dame debuted at No. 11 in the initial rankings, and the reasoning was simple."They don't have that signature win," Yurachek said Tuesday. Still, that's a bit low, right? That's a full seven spots lower than the AP poll, by far the biggest difference in the initial CFP Rankings. The loss to BYU hurts, and the Cougars' subsequent loss at UCF doesn't help, but why the disconnect from voters in the AP and coaches polls?The Irish have only one game remaining against a top 25 team: Miami this week. That win will be enough to lift the Irish into the playoff, and I suspect they will be in the top five with a victory against the Hurricanes on Saturday, but the margin for error is absolute zero. SMU tumbling out of the AP rankings with a loss to Syracuse last week hurts the Irish, who face the Mustangs later this season.
I counter with Indiana at No. 4. The Hoosiers' resume is not strong, much like their in-state rivals, so why are we rewarding the reigning national champions while punishing the Irish?This sets up another disappointment for the Irish, one way or another. Even with a win against Miami, something tells me Notre Dame could slide in the rankings in the third, fourth and fifth rankings before Selection Sunday. The committee has done it before with teams that keep winning. Heck, it happened to the Irish last season. Strength of record matters.Alabama is overratedNo. 5 Alabama is hanging its hat on a — *checks notes* — road win at Kentucky. The two-loss Tide debuted four spots higher than they were ranked in the AP and coaches polls.
The Tide are 2-2 against teams in the CFP's Top 25. The committee chairman said they were impressed by Alabama's win at Mississippi State. Huh? Remember, MSU was not at full strength; quarterback Kamario Taylor was injured, and the Bulldogs went winless in October. How is that a signature win? It meets none of the criteria the committee examines.Six — six! — teams below Alabama own better records against the CFP Top 25.We expected Kentucky to be ranked higher with one loss than Alabama with two, even with the head-to-head win. Then again, the committee doesn't weigh head-to-head results as much as we assume. Yurachek admitted that Tuesday while discussing Indiana and Ohio State's head-to-head matchup in which the Buckeyes won.Ohio State should be angryIf the playoff started today, Ohio State would not be a participant. The same Buckeyes team that defeated reigning national champion Indiana, now No. 4 in the CFP's rankings, appeared at No. 12 and the first team out of the field. 
The Buckeyes own the nation's ninth-best strength of record and 18th-best schedule, according to the same numbers ESPN flashes across the screen as they reveal the CFP rankings. Amazingly, only two Big Ten teams are in the CFP today compared to the SEC's five. Talk all you want about Ohio State playing without quarterback Julian Sayin, but the Buckeyes defeated Indiana on the road in the fourth quarter without their starter."We never got to a point where we were comparing Indiana and Ohio State in their head-to-head," Yurachek said Tuesday night.
Oh, boy. That won't sit well in Columbus, Ohio.We need to talk about UCLAUCLA is undefeated and ranks eighth. Utah is undefeated and ranks third. They're five spots apart. And there's one big difference – but it actually favors the Bruins.UCLA's strength of schedule ranks 77th. Utah is 83rd. So, why are the Bruins five spots lower? I understand Utah being higher because of its recent win against Houston, but the metrics seem to favor the Bruins elsewhere, and they've done it several weeks playing their backup quarterback.Where's New Mexico?New Mexico is the only team ranked in the AP poll (22nd) to not appear in the CFP's Top 25. That's not shocking, but why are three teams with three losses ranked above a one-loss Mountain West team whose only loss was by a touchdown on the road to the SEC's Oklahoma? After all, the committee showed Tuesday night that the SEC is the toughest conference in the country, so why isn't New Mexico rewarded with a top-25 ranking?

The SEC got a big boost from the College Football Playoff committee in the initial rankings

        No. 1 Miami led the first College Football Playoff Rankings of 2026 season as one of only three undefeated teams remaining in the sport. The Hurricanes edge out No. 2 Georgia and fellow undefeated No. 3 Utah to rank at the top. Those three teams join No. 4 Indiana from the Big Ten as the four first-round byes in the College Football Playoff. As usual, the SEC received a stunning bump of contenders compared to the AP Top 25. Alabama ranked four spots ahead of their AP ranking, coming in at No. 5 in the first CFP Rankings. Kentucky sits at No. 6 and Texas No. 7, also multiple spots ahead of their AP Poll ranking. However, the most interesting part of the bracket comes at the end. Notre Dame projects as the last time into the College Football Playoff field as the 11-seed. Powerhouse Ohio State is the first team out of the bracket at No. 12, nudged out for top Group of Six championship No. 25 Boise State. Here is a look at how the College Football playoff bracket looks after the first CFP Rankings release of the 2026 season. The schools in this scenario that would host a first-round game are No. 5 Alabama, No. 6 Kentucky, No. 7 Texas and No. 8 UCLA. The first round of the CFP would pit Texas vs. Ole Miss in a rematch and have Alabama host the Group of Six representative.  
                                                                    CBS Sports
                                                            Notre Dame must beat MiamiLast season, Notre Dame was the first team out of the College Football Playoff after finishing 10-2 with losses against two CFP squads. This year, the Fighting Irish are in an even more precarious situation coming out of the first rankings, sitting as the last team in the field. 
Notre Dame already has a loss to BYU on its schedule, and now plays No. 1 Miami on Saturday. If the Fighting Irish don't beat the top team in the nation, they're nearly a lock to miss the postseason. Notre Dame's only other potential positive data points -- SMU and Wisconsin -- both lost last weekend. They're already in the danger zone. The SEC is getting lots of creditThe CFP committee typically gives the SEC a little bump compared to the AP rankings, but this year was a whole different level. Four SEC teams ranked in the top seven of the CFP Rankings, compared to one in the AP Top 25. Alabama was the biggest winner, ranking at No. 5 in the CFP Rankings despite two losses, three spots ahead of their AP poll ranking. No. 6 Kentucky and No. 7 Texas also moved up significantly. There are five SEC teams in the projected CFP field this year, and No. 13 Tennessee and No. 14 LSU ensure that the league will get plenty of teams in. 
What would a 24-team field look like?The College Football Playoff field will be 12 teams for at least one more season, but Yahoo Sports mocked up what a larger expansion could look like. The SEC would get nine teams into the field -- more than half the league.

body:
Eight weeks into the NFL season, we're starting to get some answers about the 2026 first-round rookie class. Some players look exactly like we thought they would when they came out of college. Others have been pleasant surprises. And then there are those still struggling with some of the same issues that showed up on their college tape.We evaluated these rookies after four weeks on the With the First Pick podcast – it was our most popular episode this fall – and Arvell Reese and Sonny Styles were among the early standouts. David Bailey was still finding his footing, Rueben Bain Jr. was battling injuries, and Dillon Thieneman looked like one of the league's most promising young safeties.
A month later, some of those evaluations look a little (and, in some cases, a lot) different.These are our first-half grades for all 32 first-round picks from the 2026 class, based on everything we've seen through eight weeks. Production matters, but so do injuries, expectations and what the tape reveals. We're also revisiting our original scouting reports from the 2026 draft cycle to see which traits have translated, which concerns have followed these players to the NFL, and where we might have missed something. And because good players aren't limited to the first round, we've also graded 10 rookies drafted on Days 2 and 3 who have already made their mark.
1. Fernando Mendoza, QB, Raiders: INCOMPLETEMendoza finally got on the field in Week 5 mop-up duty vs. the Patriots. He was a tidy 6 of 8 for 48 yards. For now, veteran Kirk Cousins remains the starter, but as the losses pile up, Mendoza will likely get his chance to be QB1.2. David Bailey, EDGE, Jets: BBailey has taken a noticeable step forward after an uneven start, highlighted by a three-sack performance against Cleveland. I loved his explosive first step, speed-to-power, inside spin and relentless motor at Texas Tech, and we're seeing all of it in the NFL. What's been particularly encouraging is his development against the run, where Jets coaches have praised his discipline and ability to handle responsibilities beyond rushing the passer. He's becoming the complete defender New York envisioned when it drafted him second overall.3. Jeremiyah Love, RB, Cardinals: C+Love hasn't looked like the explosive, home-run threat we watched at Notre Dame, but there's a very simple reason: He's been battling an ankle injury since the preseason, and it cost him two games. At Notre Dame, I loved his ability to accelerate through the smallest crease and turn ordinary runs into big plays, but Love has acknowledged that he hasn't been able to cut or explode the way he did in college (not yet, anyway). This grade really doesn't mean much until we see what a healthy version of Love looks like. And that won't be for at least another month with today's trip to the IR.
4. Carnell Tate, WR, Titans: BTate is becoming a dependable target for Cam Ward despite Tennessee's offensive struggles, and that's hardly surprising given how polished he looked at Ohio State. His ability to manipulate DBs, separate at the top of routes and make difficult catches look easy gave him a chance to contribute immediately. Tate continues to get more comfortable in Tennessee's offense, and he's showing the makings of a No. 1 receiver.5. Arvell Reese, LB, Giants: A+Remember all those concerns about Reese's pro day workout? Seven months later and he's one of the easiest evaluations in the class because he's doing exactly what made him such an exciting prospect at Ohio State. Instincts, range, and insane athleticism, while learning on the job, have all made him an immediate difference-maker, and Giants coaches have praised how quickly he's hit the ground running.6. Mansoor Delane, CB, Chiefs: A-Delane looked like a grizzled All-Pro from the moment he stepped on the field. The only issue has been staying healthy. He was one of the most technically sound CBs in the draft and that has immediately translated – even when he's "allowed" receptions while in coverage (show me the human who is stopping JSN – also, look at Delane's coverage!). The Chiefs traded up for Delane and so far, it appears that they nailed this pick.
7. Sonny Styles, LB, Commanders: A+Washington already trusts Styles to relay defensive calls and make adjustments before the snap, impressive responsibilities for a rookie still relatively new to playing off-ball LB. His instincts and athleticism stood out at Ohio State, and he's carried those strengths into the NFL. He's been particularly effective in coverage vs. TEs and RBs, and he's shown consistent improvement against the run. There have been occasional missed tackles, but through eight weeks, he's been one of the best players in this rookie class.8. Jordyn Tyson, WR, Saints: INCOMPLETEThe issue with Tyson in college was staying healthy. Those issues remain.9. Spencer Fano, OT, Browns: A-Cleveland appears to have found its long-term answer at left tackle. Fano's footwork, balance and ability to recover against high-end edge rushers were some of the reasons I liked him so much coming out of Utah. And even though he's moved from right to left tackle for the Browns, he's doing a lot of the same things really well. 10. Francis Mauigoa, OG, Giants: C+The move from college tackle to NFL guard hasn't been seamless, but Mauigoa has steadily gotten better. His athleticism and ability to move defenders in the running game stood out at Miami, although he occasionally struggled with balance and hand placement. Those issues have followed him inside, but his improved pass protection, especially vs. Houston in Week 7, was encouraging.
11. Caleb Downs, S, Cowboys: C+Few prospects were easier to trust coming out of college than Downs, whose instincts, anticipation and IQ made him special at Ohio State. This is what makes his recent NFL struggles so surprising (I gave him a B+ through the first month of the season). Opponents have completed 20 of 24 passes against him for 230 yards and three touchdowns, and poor pursuit angles have contributed to explosive runs. Dallas expected a defensive centerpiece, not a liability in coverage, as CBS Sports' Garrett Podell detailed.12. Kadyn Proctor, OG, Dolphins: C+Proctor has been candid about his struggles moving inside, acknowledging that speed of the game in confined spaces -- something he didn't have to deal with at Alabama -- creates bigger problems at guard. His rare athleticism remains obvious, but the balance and hand-placement concerns from his college tape haven't disappeared. A Week 7 concussion hasn't helped, keeping him sidelined for Week 8's loss to the Patriots.13. Ty Simpson, QB, Rams: INCOMPLETERemember when we all gawked and pointed at the Rams' arrogance for taking Simpson when there were bigger, more immediate needs? I suppose that case can still be made … but it also doesn't look like Matthew Stafford has another year or two left in him. 
14. Olaivavega Ioane, OG, Ravens: B+Baltimore has already needed Ioane to play center because of injuries, and he's handled the transition well. His powerful hands, leverage and ability to anchor made him one of my favorite interior linemen at Penn State. He's brought that same reliability to Baltimore, although an MCL injury has interrupted an otherwise encouraging start. And while our old buddy Rick Spielman wasn't a fan of plus/minus when grading players, I'm giving Ioane an extra plus for his versatility. 15. Rueben Bain Jr., EDGE, Buccaneers: CIt's taken a bit, but we're finally seeing the player who was a game wrecker at Miami. Shoulder and groin injuries derailed Bain's first month, but his explosive first step, violent hands and ability to generate power are showing up more consistently as he gets healthy. The production hasn't matched expectations yet, although he's trending in the right direction.16. Kenyon Sadiq, TE, Jets: B-Remember Sadiq's seven-catch, 105-yard performance against Detroit? That's the explosive mismatch weapon we saw at Oregon. But his opportunities have diminished with Mason Taylor back in the lineup, and a Week 5 concussion only complicated matters. The encouraging part? His blocking has been better than expected, even if the receiving production hasn't followed.
17. Blake Miller, OT, Lions: BMiller's pass protection has been one of the more encouraging developments among all rookie offensive linemen. His balance, lateral agility and ability to redirect stood out at Clemson, and he's handled NFL edge rushers surprisingly well over the first two months. The running game is another story; he hasn't been nearly as good play in and play out.18. Caleb Banks, DT, Vikings: INCOMPLETEMinnesota knew Banks was a developmental prospect, but he's played just 25% of the defensive snaps and hasn't made much of an impact. When healthy, his twitch, lateral quickness and ability to penetrate made him a lot of fun to watch at Florida. The problem? Once blockers get their hands on him, particularly on double teams, he struggles to disengage. Those concerns haven't disappeared, and his limited playing time suggests the Vikings aren't ready to trust him with a bigger role. I'm giving Banks an incomplete here, in part because we knew this would be a process, in part because Dallas Turner needed a couple of years in Brian Flores' system before figuring it out.19. Monroe Freeling, OT, Panthers: C-Freeling deserves credit for responding well when Carolina needed him earlier than expected, and at a position (RT) he didn't play in college. A knee injury hasn't helped his development,  and right now, he's more of a developmental prospect than a reliable starter.
20. Makai Lemon, WR, Eagles: B-After a quiet September that left a lot of folks wondering if Sean Mannion knew Lemon was on the roster, the USC standout is finally starting to look like the first-round talent we saw last fall for the Trojans. His toughness, reliable hands and ability to create after the catch have become more evident as his role expands. There have been some drops, but he's one of the few bright spots in an otherwise forgettable season in Philly.21. Max Iheanachor, OT, Steelers: B-Iheanachor hasn't avoided rookie mistakes, but what's encouraging is how he's responded to them. His quick feet, power and lateral movement skills were obvious at Arizona State, even if he was incredibly raw. He's still raw, but he's shown an ability to quickly make adjustments instead of repeating the same mistakes.22. Akheem Mesidor, EDGE, Chargers: BDespite all that's gone wrong with the Chargers, Mesidor has been one of the bright spots, and his coaches have explained why: he's stopped overthinking and started trusting his instincts. The heavy hands, leverage, versatility and non-stop motor that made him a first-rounder out of Miami are showing up more consistently. He's playing faster, even if the production doesn't always reflect it.
23. Malachi Lawrence, EDGE, Cowboys: C-Lawrence's first NFL sack offered a glimpse of the explosiveness that made him stand out at UCF. His first-step quickness and power were impressive in college, but limited bend meant he'd need to develop better counters and hand usage. That's all still a work in progress, and the reality is that Dallas hasn't gotten consistent production from him. In his defense, they've gotten consistent production from exactly no one on this defense.24. KC Concepcion, WR, Browns: B+Concepcion has been better than advertised and the advertisements were pretty good coming out of Texas A&M. His suddenness and precise route running have immediately translated. Browns coaches have also praised his preparation and ability to learn multiple receiver positions, giving Cleveland more ways to get him involved. GM Andrew Berry has quietly crushed another draft class.25. Dillon Thieneman, S, Bears: B-A month ago, Thieneman looked like one of the pleasant surprises of Round 1 (I gave him a B+ at the quarter pole). His instincts, range and willingness to attack downhill were everything we saw at Oregon. But the concerns about flipping his hips and tracking receivers downfield have resurfaced, and now opponents are increasingly testing him vertically. His second month hasn't been nearly as impressive as his first, but there's still a ton to be excited about.
26. Keylan Rutledge, OG, Texans: C-Houston drafted Rutledge to add some much-needed nastiness up front, but his pass protection has been a problem. To be fair, the Texans have asked him to learn all three interior o-line positions after playing almost exclusively right guard at Georgia Tech. Still, poor balance, hand placement and recognition have made him vulnerable, and the physical tools remain more impressive than the results. Overall, I'm going to grade him on a curve because he's been asked to do a lot in a short span.27. Chris Johnson, CB, Dolphins: C+Johnson is becoming more dependable as Miami moves him between outside corner and the slot. His competitiveness, recovery speed and ability to stay in phase on shorter routes were strengths at San Diego State, and we're seeing that now show up on Sundays. Bottom line: He's made real progress since September, when I gave him a C.28. Caleb Lomu, OT, Patriots: INCOMPLETELomu has played only about 160 snaps -- far fewer than most of the first-round rookie offensive linemen -- but he's made the most of his opportunities. He was impressive against the Jets in Week 6. Filling in for an injured Morgan Moses, he played 60 snaps at right tackle, allowed zero pressures and held his own against David Bailey. His quick feet and balance were strengths at Utah, and they're serving him well as he adjusts to the NFL. I gave him an incomplete here but if pressed, I'd give him a B-.29. Peter Woods, DT, Chiefs: C+Woods was one of the most physically gifted defenders in this class, which makes his uneven start a little frustrating. His explosiveness, leverage and ability to disrupt running plays have translated from Clemson, but he hasn't been nearly as effective rushing the passer. He still struggles with double teams, and his inability to consistently win one-on-one as a pass rusher remains a concern.30. Omar Cooper Jr., WR, Jets: A-Two consecutive 100-yard games after returning from injured reserve? That'll work. Cooper's toughness, contested-catch ability and knack for making difficult receptions look routine were how he made his name at Indiana. He's already developing chemistry with Geno Smith, and while it's a small sample, there's a lot to like.31. Keldric Faulk, EDGE, Titans: D+Faulk's length and power made him an appealing first-round prospect at Auburn, but he hasn't consistently turned those tools into on-field production. An early sack against the Giants offered a glimpse of his potential. Since then, he's struggled when OTs have neutralized his initial pass-rush move. He'll need to diversify his pass-rush arsenal, something that showed up on tape in college but was less of an issue because he was routinely the freakiest athlete on the field. 32. Jadarian Price, RB, Seahawks: INCOMPLETEPrice's chest injury has left us with little to evaluate. He got off to a promising start in Week 1, rushing for 52 yards on 10 carries, but played just two more games before landing on injured reserve. He also lost fumbles in both of those appearances. The talent we saw at Notre Dame is still there, but we've barely seen it in Seattle.Of course, the first round isn't the only place teams find impact players. Here are some Day 2 names who have stood out through the first half of their rookie seasons -- and in some cases, are already outperforming players drafted well ahead of them.Beyond the first round: Ten more rookies already making a markDenzel Boston, WR, Browns (Round 2): B+Boston has given Cleveland a legitimate downfield threat, with 409 receiving yards and three touchdowns through eight games. His size, body control and ability to win contested catches have translated from Washington, although defenses have done a better job limiting his explosive plays recently.Jacob Rodriguez, LB, Dolphins (Round 2): A-Rodriguez has wasted little time becoming an important part of Miami's defense, relying on the instincts, play recognition and tackling ability that made him so productive at Texas Tech. He may not have elite athletic traits, but he consistently finds the football and has been one of the more impressive second-round rookies.Gabe Jacas, EDGE, Patriots (Round 2): A-Jacas has been a problem for opposing offensive tackles, generating 21 pressures through his first seven games. His power, bend and ability to diagnose plays have stood out on film, and he's already producing like a player who should have been drafted higher.Emmanuel McNeil-Warren, S, Browns (Round 2): B+McNeil-Warren has earned an expanding role in Cleveland's secondary, where his length, physicality, closing speed and versatility have helped the Browns disguise coverages. The instincts and willingness to attack downhill that stood out at Toledo are serving him well, and he's developing into a valuable piece of the defense.Germie Bernard, WR, Steelers (Round 2): B+Bernard has taken advantage of Pittsburgh's injuries at receiver, becoming an increasingly reliable target for Aaron Rodgers. His route awareness, toughness, blocking and ability to line up in multiple spots have translated from Alabama, while his preparation and willingness to learn have earned praise from the coaching staff.And then there are the Day 3 picks, where finding immediate contributors becomes a little more difficult -- and sometimes the evaluations look a lot different with the benefit of hindsight. For these five rookies, I've included my original pre-draft grade, final big board ranking and what I liked about them coming out of college, if only to see what I got right, what I missed and whether these teams saw something I didn't.Gracen Halton, DT, 49ers (Round 4): A-My pre-draft grade: 3rd–4th round | Final big board rank: No. 98Why I liked him: An explosive, one-gap penetrator with surprising power, active hands and a relentless motor who could disrupt plays before offensive linemen established their blocks.Halton has been one of the biggest Day 3 steals, making an immediate impact on San Francisco's defensive line with 15 tackles, two sacks and a forced fumble through six games. His first-step quickness, ability to disengage from blockers and relentless motor have all helped him become an integral part of the rotation.Keionte Scott, DB, Buccaneers (Round 4): A-My pre-draft grade: 3rd round | Final big board rank: No. 84Why I liked him: A physical, aggressive slot defender who could cover, blitz off the edge and blow up running plays near the line of scrimmage.Scott might be the best example of a Day 3 rookie playing well beyond his draft position (though he slipped on draft day because of off-field concerns). He's already established himself as Tampa Bay's starting nickel, where his physicality, quick trigger and versatility have made him a valuable part of Todd Bowles' defense. Bowles has praised his toughness and tackling.Dani Dennis-Sutton, EDGE, Packers (Round 4): B+My pre-draft grade: 4th round | Final big board rank: No. 122Why I liked him: A powerful, high-motor edge defender with heavy hands, a strong lower half and the ability to set the edge against the run.Dennis-Sutton has given Green Bay valuable pass-rush production, generating 15 pressures through seven weeks and earning more playing time as a result. His power, heavy hands and ability to hold up against the run were obvious at Penn State, but he's also shown more as a pass rusher than I expected.Jaden Dugger, LB, 49ers (Round 5): B+My pre-draft grade: 7th–UDFA | Final big board rank: No. 300Why I liked him: A physical, downhill linebacker with length, straight-line speed and the willingness to take on blockers, although his lateral stiffness and coverage limitations were significant concerns.Dugger has become a valuable part of San Francisco's defense, playing more than half the defensive snaps and recording 30 tackles through seven games. A former safety still learning the nuances of off-ball LB, he's making excellent use of his range, closing speed and versatility, with the coaching staff trusting him in coverage and as a blitzer. Also goes to show that sometimes one person's evaluation can miss the mark (and sometimes by a good bit).Kendal Daniels, LB, Falcons (Round 4): B+My pre-draft grade: 4th round | Final big board rank: No. 134Why I liked him: A versatile hybrid defender with outstanding range, physicality and some of the best open-field tackling ability in the class, capable of making plays from the slot, box or edge.One of my 2026 draft sleepers, Daniels has been one of the most impressive Day 3 picks of the class, starting all eight games with 53 tackles, four tackles for loss, a sack and an interception. His range, versatility and ability to finish tackles in space were among the reasons I thought he might sneak into Day 2, and he's already becoming an important part of Jeff Ulbrich's defense.
